{"id": "18:34/q10", "question": "What does the claim of more wealth mean?", "turns_on": "How literally to take the comparative against the narratives of the believer's poverty and equal inheritance.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q10/p1", "position": "The garden owner claims greater property than his companion.", "reasons": "The contrast follows his abundant gardens and other assets; Ṭabarī calls the companion poorer. Muqātil adds his fine clothes and mount against the believer's worn state. Al-Kashshāf says extra gold and silver enabled him to develop land, and Biqāʿī says it enabled labor and tools."}, {"id": "18:34/q10/p2", "position": "The comparison appears literal and implies the companion had some wealth and followers.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān uses the comparative text against historical accounts of a destitute petitioner. Bursevī and Ālūsī point to the tension with reports that the brothers inherited equal shares and the believer gave his away; Bursevī leaves it unresolved."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q11", "question": "How are مالا and نفرا construed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q11/p1", "position": "Both are accusative specifications of the comparative degree.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Ālūsī label both accusative specifications; Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly calls nafaran specification of the comparison."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q12", "question": "What does أعز express in the boast?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q12/p1", "position": "Greater strength, honor and social standing.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr links strength and honor to numerous courageous kin. Others summarize it as a stronger retinue, clan or greater status."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q13", "question": "What is omitted after أعز, and how does the comparative work?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q13/p1", "position": "The second comparative inherits the standard منك from the first.", "reasons": "Burhān says omitted comparison standards are often inferred when afʿal is a predicate; it compares 87:17. The same source outlines construct, definite and unmarked-plus-min patterns and conditions for definite, plural and collective nouns after afʿal, citing 63:8, 26:111, 18:103, 6:123 and 11:27."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q14", "question": "Who are the owner's نفر?", "turns_on": "Whether social power is counted by dependents, male offspring, or the wider kin group; later references to offspring favor the first two for some authors.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q14/p1", "position": "His retainers, servants and attendants.", "reasons": "Qatāda and Ibn ʿAbbās identify servants; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this reading permits the two men to be brothers. Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers servants and children by the later comparison at 18:39. Some combine attendants with children."}, {"id": "18:34/q14/p2", "position": "His children, especially sons.", "reasons": "Muqātil adduces the later mention of wealth and offspring (18:39); Ibn ʿĀshūr cites verse 40. Al-Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī and Nasafī explain that sons accompany their father unlike daughters. Some pair sons with servants and helpers."}, {"id": "18:34/q14/p3", "position": "His clan, kinsmen and fighting supporters.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim and Abū Sulaymān take clan; Rāzī says they defend and accompany him. Ṭabrisī says the group accompanies him on errands; Ibn Qutayba's examples present many brothers as protection and support for the back. Some sources combine clan and general retinue."}, {"id": "18:34/q14/p4", "position": "A small group of men, conventionally three to ten.", "reasons": "Ibn Fāris gives three to ten, comparing qawm and rahṭ as collectives without a singular of the same form. Qurtubī says fewer than ten, and Bursevī specifies male helpers and an upper limit of ten."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q15", "question": "What background is reported for the two men and their garden?", "turns_on": "Whether the parable is a specific historical incident, a differently located tale, or a general figure; names, sums and settings vary across reports.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q15/p1", "position": "They were brothers who inherited wealth; the believer spent for God and the unbeliever built worldly prosperity.", "reasons": "Muqātil has the impoverished believer seek generosity and describe lending his inheritance to God for himself and his children; the unbeliever mocks him. Māwardī contrasts afterlife spending with status seeking. Qurtubī recounts charity, mosque building, the believer seeking work and being expelled after resurrection was denied; another account details heavenly land, house, wife and servants. Jishumī connects the story with 37:50."}, {"id": "18:34/q15/p2", "position": "They were Meccan Makhzūmī brothers, Abū Salama and al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī says each inherited four thousand dinars and the believer spent his share for God; Qurtubī cites 37:51."}, {"id": "18:34/q15/p3", "position": "They were Israelite brothers, the believer Judah or Tamlīkha and unbeliever Qarṭūsh.", "reasons": "Qurtubī attributes Judah to Ibn ʿAbbās and Tamlīkha/Qarṭūsh to Muqātil; the names vary in the reports."}, {"id": "18:34/q15/p4", "position": "They were partners with eight thousand dinars.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ supplies the partnership and sum."}, {"id": "18:34/q15/p5", "position": "The gardens were at Lake Tinnīs, which flooded overnight.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports that one brother sold his share, spent in obedience and was mocked before the lake flooded."}, {"id": "18:34/q15/p6", "position": "The wealthy owner is Fatrus or Qutrus.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī calls him Fatrus and depicts his tour, boast, doubt in the Hour and hope of a better return; Nasafī calls him Qutrus. These are name variants in the accounts."}, {"id": "18:34/q15/p7", "position": "A fishing test and an angelic vision expose the difference between worldly luck and final fate.", "reasons": "Qurtubī says the unbeliever caught many fish invoking an idol while the believer caught none invoking God; an angel protested, and Gabriel showed each man's abode, so both judged earthly fortune irrelevant. God took the believer and ruined the unbeliever, who was seen in Hell as in 37:51–52."}, {"id": "18:34/q15/p8", "position": "The parable may be a general example for this community rather than an account of particular men.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports it as an exhortation to renounce worldly life and desire the hereafter; Qurtubī says the context argues against this."}, {"id": "18:34/q15/p9", "position": "The pair can stand for the Prophet and Meccans, believers and disbelievers, or ʿUyayna's party and Salmān's.", "reasons": "Qurtubī reports these further identifications alongside the link with 37:51; they are separate generalized applications grouped here as variants rather than an agreed historical identification."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q16", "question": "How does this verse fit the surrounding parable and other verses?", "turns_on": "The sources compare the boast with adjacent admonition, a later eschatological dialogue, and the parable's destruction.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q16/p1", "position": "The boast answers the earlier call to remain with believers and exposes the arrogance of rich opponents.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya compare ʿUyayna and al-Aqraʿ asking the Prophet to dismiss Salmān, Khabbāb and Ṣuhayb as inferior; Qurtubī links the parable to patience with believers at 18:28. Abū Ḥayyān likens the pride to Quraysh leaders; Iṣlāḥī sees Quraysh's outward and inward arrogance."}, {"id": "18:34/q16/p2", "position": "The worldly exchange here has an afterlife counterpart in 37:51–61.", "reasons": "Qurtubī says the latter describes the brothers' afterlife situation, with the believer recalling his companion in Hell; Jishumī also connects the inherited-wealth account with 37:50."}, {"id": "18:34/q16/p3", "position": "The garden's collapse later demonstrates the error of trusting wealth and followers.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the companion refutes the claim verbally and ruin demonstrates it. Iṣlāḥī contrasts the owner's assumption of indestructibility with Dhū al-Qarnayn's gratitude and trust in God's promise."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q17", "question": "What does the owner's boast teach about wealth and status?", "turns_on": "The outward moral of worldly pretension and an inward symbolic reading of its images.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q17/p1", "position": "Worldly wealth and strong followers can feed arrogance and are no proof of lasting divine favor.", "reasons": "Qatāda calls them the wicked person's ambition; Qushayrī says the unbeliever failed to thank his Provider and regretted ruin. Iṣlāḥī says opponents treat prosperity as proof of belief and expect a better hereafter. Study Quran compares 18:46, 9:55, 9:85, 23:55–56, 3:10, 3:116, 9:69, 26:88 and 34:35, arguing wealth and children cannot shield punishment. Ṭabāṭabāʾī has the later ruin refute self-sufficiency."}, {"id": "18:34/q17/p2", "position": "In an inward reading, the gardens and fruit represent worldly desire and cravings.", "reasons": "Al-Nīsābūrī maps wealth and status to blameworthy traits, imagined better return to delusion about God, and turning hands in regret to wasted life and good potential."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q18", "question": "What details about the gardens before the boast are supplied?", "turns_on": "The immediately preceding garden description and whether its word for 'both' is singular in form or genuinely dual.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q18/p1", "position": "The two gardens bore full produce, with palms, crops and flowing water.", "reasons": "Qurtubī describes palms encircling them, grapes and crops, and a river through the middle; ḥifāf means an encircling edge. Jishumī says the gardens contained other trees too. Ṭabrisī describes the later calamity erasing their green growth."}, {"id": "18:34/q18/p2", "position": "The preceding كلتا is grammatically singular in form while denoting two gardens.", "reasons": "Qurtubī cites singular ātat and Jarīr

Qurtubī compares naḥnu as singular form for multiple referents."}, {"id": "18:34/q18/p3", "position": "The preceding كلتا is a dual derived from كل.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says lām is lightened and dual alif added; it is always annexed and has no standalone singular. Basrans and Qurtubī dispute the analysis from case and agreement."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q19", "question": "What ancillary examples of wording and authority appear in the collected excerpts?", "turns_on": "These excerpts concern separate cited examples and are not direct interpretations of the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q19/p1", "position": "Sentence conjunction depends on the strength of the connection.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī says adjective/noun or emphasis form such a unity that conjunction would coordinate a thing with itself; distinct sentences sharing syntactic role are conjoined; wholly unrelated sentences are not. Omitting conjunction may indicate maximal connection or complete separation."}, {"id": "18:34/q19/p2", "position": "Fronting an object challenges the target's fitness for the action.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī's example a-Zaydan taḍrib questions whether anyone would dare strike Zayd."}, {"id": "18:34/q19/p3", "position": "Several lexical and proverbial explanations address support, relief and hidden danger.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba glosses taṣfarr as lacking affection, makfūfa as folded and supported by Shammākh, and prophetic nafas as relief through the Anṣār. He transmits ʿUmar's wind from God's rūḥ, Abū Bakr's 'handful' image for numbers small before God, and competing small-cave versus water-source senses of al-Ghuwayr, one attributed to Bihays."}, {"id": "18:34/q19/p4", "position": "Public consultation is necessary for a ruler's pledge.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba reports ʿUmar saying a private pledge establishes neither man as ruler and could leave both liable to be killed; authority requires the gathering's assent."}, {"id": "18:34/q19/p5", "position": "The Qurʾān itself proves the Prophet's mission by its miraculous composition.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī says God made the Prophet's heart repository of revelation but could withhold it, and the Qurʾān establishes its divine source. Other scriptures need another sign because their composition is not miraculous, though their unseen reports may be; Moses knew speech directly, reciters know by inference."}, {"id": "18:34/q19/p6", "position": "ʿUthmān defended his rule against suspicious faultfinders.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports ʿUthmān describing public flatterers who concealed hostility and followed first callers, arguing that they accepted ʿUmar despite greater complaints because he restrained them, and asserting the imam's claim to act."}]}
{"id": "18:34/q20", "question": "What other historical reports are present among the collected excerpts?", "turns_on": "These are separate historical excerpts included in the source notes rather than positions on the garden parable.", "positions": [{"id": "18:34/q20/p1", "position": "Moses, Aaron and the Night Journey are described in distinct reports.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān reports Moses as tall, dark and curly-haired and al-Thaʿlabī gives his lifespan as 120. Aaron's kinship is disputed between full, maternal or paternal brother; he is described as taller and eloquent, born a year earlier and dying first. A Night Journey report places him in the fifth heaven with half-white beard; Ibn Miskawayh glosses his Hebrew name as 'beloved.'"}, {"id": "18:34/q20/p2", "position": "David's lineage, appearance and reign are reported.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān lists his ancestry through Jesse, Judah and Jacob; al-Tirmidhī/Kaʿb describe his devotion, appearance, voice and prophethood with kingship; al-Nawawī reports 100 years of life, 40 of rule and twelve sons."}, {"id": "18:34/q20/p3", "position": "Solomon's qualities and reign are reported.", "reasons": "Kaʿb describes his appearance, devotion, humility and early consultation by his father. Ibn ʿAbbās names him and Dhū al-Qarnayn among believing world kings, against Nimrod and Nebuchadnezzar. Historians give accession at thirteen, Temple building four years later and death at fifty-three."}, {"id": "18:34/q20/p4", "position": "Job's lineage is uncertain, with different reports.", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq says only his father Abyad is secure; Ibn Jarīr traces him through Esau to Isaac; Ibn ʿAsākir makes his mother Lot's daughter and his father Abraham's believer, placing him before Moses."}, {"id": "18:34/q20/p5", "position": "Accounts of early conversions and teaching in Yathrib are excerpted.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports ʿUmar hearing Ṭā Hā after learning his sister and her husband converted, then accepting Islam. After al-ʿAqaba the Prophet sent Muṣʿab to Yathrib to teach with Asʿad, and Usayd arrived armed to confront them at Saʿd's request."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q01", "question": "What happened when the man entered his garden?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q01/p1", "position": "He led his believing companion through the garden to show off its beauty and wealth.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports the commentators and Ibn al-Jawzī say he took his Muslim brother by the hand; al-Kashshāf names the owner Qaṭrus and says he showed both gardens and boasted of wealth; al-Baghawī specifies fruit; al-Bayḍāwī says they toured together. Al-Qurṭubī reports this as one account. Bursawī says Qaṭrus showed one garden to his brother; Iṣlāḥī stresses that the entrance accompanied proud speech."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q02", "question": "Why is his garden singular although he has two?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular marks sequential physical entry, a connected pair, or all the owner's worldly possessions; the Hudhalī grammatical analogy and the entry narrative are disputed.", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q02/p1", "position": "He entered one of the two gardens at a time.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say simultaneous entry into both is impossible; Ibn ʿĀshūr says he entered one first. Al-Nasafī allows one of the pair, while al-Bayḍāwī, Bursawī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī give successive entry as one explanation. Abū Ḥayyān calls this the meaning of the report and objects to al-Zamakhsharī's collective reading."}, {"id": "18:35/q02/p2", "position": "The two adjoining gardens count as one orchard or a collective garden.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā and al-Suddī describe one orchard divided by a river; al-Nasafī mentions a shared wall despite the river. Al-Bayḍāwī and Bursawī cite adjacency; al-Farrāʾ cites this verse's singular for treating the pair as one; al-Biqāʿī calls the singular generic. Abū al-Baqāʾ takes one for a pair and cites a Hudhalī verse, but al-Samīn says its pronouns agree with a broken plural; al-Ālūsī calls al-Suddī's account unpersuasive. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī permits a generic singular."}, {"id": "18:35/q02/p3", "position": "His sole garden is his whole worldly estate, with no share in the promised Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says neither individual orchard is specifically designated; al-Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān report the same contrast with Paradise. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī include it; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it subtle. Al-Samīn replies to the Sheikh's objection that al-Zamakhsharī need not mean simultaneous entry. Al-Ālūsī prefers this collective sense because context has the companion entering with him; Abū Ḥayyān rejects it in favor of entry into one garden."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q03", "question": "To whom do the pronouns in the passage refer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q03/p1", "position": "The four pronouns refer to the garden owner.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī states this explicitly while explaining the singular garden as generic, successive entry, or the worldly pair together."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q04", "question": "How does the clause 'while wronging himself' work grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q04/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause of the subject of 'entered,' with 'to himself' governed by 'wronging.'", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says the lām is additional because ẓālim is a derived governing form. Al-Ālūsī also identifies the phrase as circumstantial and connects it to the danger of disbelief and lost blessings."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q05", "question": "In what way was he wronging himself?", "turns_on": "The notes variously name disbelief and resurrection denial, ingratitude for God's gift, and pride or reliance on wealth; several combine them.", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q05/p1", "position": "He disbelieved in God, associated partners with Him, or denied resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says he left faith for disbelief; Qatāda and Ibn Zayd add corrupt beliefs and doubt about rising. Al-Zajjāj says disbelief consigns a person to lasting Fire, the gravest self-wrong. Other sources add disobedience, rebellion, vanity, weak certainty and reliance on visible causes; Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies shirk and denial of resurrection. Al-Jishumī explains the related word radd as returning oneself to unbelief."}, {"id": "18:35/q05/p2", "position": "He was ungrateful for God's favor and used blessings for boasting instead of gratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says admiration and boasting exposed him to divine anger; al-Rāzī says the clause interrupts the story to show misuse of blessings for ingratitude and denial of resurrection. Qatāda in al-Durr calls it ingratitude for his Lord's favor. Al-Ālūsī says he misplaced gratitude and humility; the Study Quran cites 3:117 and 10:44 for self-wronging through sin and disbelief."}, {"id": "18:35/q05/p3", "position": "He was conceited, proud of his wealth, and relied on it rather th

an on his Lord.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī combines conceit with disbelief; al-Biqāʿī says wealth displaced reliance on God. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds pride toward his companion, self-admiration and latent shirk through forgetting God; Iṣlāḥī describes proud speech, and the Study Quran says he refused to acknowledge God as provider. Al-Nīsābūrī gives an inward reading of wealth and status as blameworthy inclinations."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q06", "question": "Why is his speech introduced after the account of his entry?", "turns_on": "Whether the later companion's speech is another circumstantial clause or a new explanatory sentence.", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q06/p1", "position": "The speech explains the self-wrong and answers the implied question of what he said.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the speech answers a question prompted by the unjust entry; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says its clause is separated for an implied question. Al-Rāzī calls the self-wronging description an interruption that exposes ingratitude and resurrection denial. Al-Samīn prefers a new explanatory clause for the later companion's speech over treating it as circumstantial."}, {"id": "18:35/q06/p2", "position": "The later 'his companion said' may be circumstantial.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn records this possibility for qāla lahu ṣāḥibuhu, but prefers a new explanatory clause."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q07", "question": "What force does 'I do not think' have here?", "turns_on": "Whether ẓann retains a sense of supposition or conveys practical certainty.", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q07/p1", "position": "It expresses supposition or lack of certainty.", "reasons": "Muqātil glosses aẓunnu as 'suppose'; Yaḥyā ibn Sallām explains it as 'I am not certain.'"}, {"id": "18:35/q07/p2", "position": "Ẓann can convey knowledge or near certainty; he could hardly conceive the garden's end.", "reasons": "Bursawī says ẓann is often borrowed for knowledge or near certainty. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the negative form portrays permanence as so secure that destruction does not enter his mind."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q08", "question": "How do grammarians analyze the construction after 'I think'?", "turns_on": "Whether an indefinite licenses the separation pronoun; negation changes the indefinite's force.", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q08/p1", "position": "An indefinite cannot be followed by huwa as a separation pronoun in this construction.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives the Basran objection: an indefinite cannot take the relevant adjective or apposition. He cites lā yastaqīm aẓunnu rajulan khayran minka, while negation allows an indefinite with the force of aḥad. Yūnus reports Abū ʿAmr judged the usage ungrammatical and calls Ibn Marwān's accusative reading of 15:71 an error; al-Khalīl regards huwa as a genuine pronoun like abūhu, not an empty particle like mā, even between definites."}, {"id": "18:35/q08/p2", "position": "Huwa can be a separation pronoun after an indefinite by analogy with definites.", "reasons": "Sībawayh reports this as the Medinan grammarians' analysis; the Basrans, Abū ʿAmr, and al-Khalīl object on syntactic grounds."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q09", "question": "What does 'perish' mean and how is its verb formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q09/p1", "position": "Bāda yabīdu means perish, disappear, or be destroyed; its verbal nouns include bayd, biyūd, and baydūda.", "reasons": "Muqātil glosses tabīda as perish. Al-Jishumī gives bayd and also the sense 'except'; Abū Ḥayyān gives baydūda and cites poetry where bāda means a household perished. Al-Samīn gives biyūdan and baydūdatan, analyzing the latter as fayʿalūla after deletion of one yāʾ, like kaynūna. Bursawī says disappear; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says destruction and extinction; Ibn ʿĀshūr says perish. Sībawayh pairs bādat tabīdu biyūdan with ghābat al-shams ghuyūban and strong-root julūs and nufūr."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q10", "question": "What wider morphology illustrates the verbal noun of tabīda?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q10/p1", "position": "Medially weak verbs have several verbal-noun and participle patterns, including the verse's bādat tabīdu biyūdan.", "reasons": "Sībawayh compares bādat with ghābat and regular julūs/nufūr. He surveys bayʿ/kayl with bāʾiʿ/kāʾil, ziyāra/ʿiyāda/ḥiyāka avoiding faʿūl, khawf/khāʾif and transitive analogies, nayl/dhām/ʿāb or ʿayb, sūʾ/qūt and ʿiyāfa, suʾūr/ghuʾūr, qiyām/ṣiyām/iyāb, other yāʾ-root alternatives, dawām/zawāl/rawāḥ, and lāʿ versus lāʾiʿ. Al-Akhṭal's line attests suʾūr; al-ʿAjjāj's line attests its hollow-verb form. Sībawayh compares strong-root forms throughout and notes both wāw and yāʾ roots can avoid faʿūl."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q11", "question": "What does 'this' designate in his claim?", "turns_on": "Whether the demonstrative reaches beyond the visible orchard to the world's created order.", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q11/p1", "position": "It designates the garden he entered, or its fruit.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān explicitly identifies the demonstrative with the garden entered. Al-Ṭabrisī allows the garden and its fruit; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī also says the destruction spoken of is the garden. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this narrow reference would express shallow arrogance rather than a theory about cosmic order."}, {"id": "18:35/q11/p2", "position": "It designates the whole world or cosmos.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī gives this as an alternative; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it would be doubt about the cosmos's created order. Al-Jishumī reports that the man may be denying that the world ends. Al-Wāḥidī and al-Zajjāj take him to deny the world's passing. Abū Ḥayyān calls a cosmic reference remote, and al-Ālūsī rejects cosmic readings as strained."}]}
{"id": "18:35/q12", "question": "How long did he think the garden would last?", "turns_on": "Whether abad is literal eternity, the man's lifetime or another very long span, and whether the claim concerns the orchard or the cosmos.", "positions": [{"id": "18:35/q12/p1", "position": "He imagined the garden would never perish at all.", "reasons": "Muqātil reports the plain claim; al-Baghawī connects it with denial of the Hour. Al-Wāḥidī says the thriving garden led him to deny God's power to end this world. Al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Suddī report the same boast; Ibn Kathīr cites flourishing crops and streams, weak certainty and attachment to this life. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it a settled assumption of permanence; Iṣlāḥī calls the garden lush and the belief arrogant."}, {"id": "18:35/q12/p2", "position": "He expected it to survive for his own lifetime, with 'forever' meaning that long span.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan denies that he meant literal eternity and compares 104:3, wealth's supposed power to immortalize. Sallam, al-Thaʿlabi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir, and others identify the speaker by his faith and the addressee as the owner; Ibn ʿAshur says he had already admonished the rich man, who answered arrogantly."}, {"id": "18:37/q01/p2", "position": "Sahib here means brother.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi attributes this gloss to some exegetes."}, {"id": "18:37/q01/p3", "position": "The believing companion was called Judah.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi gives Judah as one of the disputed names."}, {"id": "18:37/q01/p4", "position": "The believing companion was called Tamlīkha.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi gives Tamlīkha as the alternative disputed name."}]}
{"id": "18:37/q02", "question": "Why does the companion's speech begin without a conjunction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:37/q02/p1", "position": "The bare qāla introduces the answering turn in the dialogue.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur treats the speech as a question-and-answer turn."}]}
{"id": "18:37/q03", "question": "How are the hāʾ pronouns in this phrase used?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:37/q03/p1", "position": "The hāʾ is an ordinary third-person pronoun occurring in genitive or accusative position.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān and al-Itqān cite the companion's speech phrase as an example; the former notes both cases, and the latter specifically glosses 'his companion said to him.'"}]}
{"id": "18:37/q04", "question": "What does yuḥāwiruhu mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the conversation is described neutrally or as dispute; the dispute wording is reported as an explanatory reading.", "positions": [{"id": "18:37/q04/p1", "position": "He was speaking or conversing with him.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda derives it from muḥāwara, conversation; al-Tabatabaʾi takes the repeated dialogue wording as showing the believer's steady composure and gentle speech."}, {"id": "18:37/q04/p2", "position": "He was disputing with him.", "reasons": "Ubayy's explanatory wording yukhāṣimuhu expresses this sense; Ibn ʿAtiyya reports it, while Abū Ḥayyān says it is explanatory and not transmitted recitation because it differs from the codex."}]}
{"id": "18:37/q05", "question": "What status has Ubayy's wording wa-huwa yukhāṣimuhu?", "turns_on": "Whether Ubayy's differing wording counts as recitation or explanation in light of the codex.", "positions": [{"id": "18:37/q05/p1", "position": "It is reported as Ubayy's wording describing a dispute.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya and al-Ālūsī report Ubayy's wording."}, {"id": "18:37/q05/p2", "position": "It is only explanatory, not a transmitted Qur'anic recitation.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says the received reading is yuḥāwiruhu and Ubayy's wording differs from the codex."}]}
{"id": "18:37/q06", "question": "What is the syntax of wa-huwa yuḥāwiruhu?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:37/q06/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause describing the believing speaker.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān identifies it as a ḥāl; al-Ālūsī calls it an independent circumstantial clause framing the exchange."}]}
{"id": "18:37/q07", "question": "Why is their conversation explicitly mentioned?", "turns_on": "Whether the dialogue phrase chiefly draws attention to the speech or characterizes the believer's manner.", "positions": [{"id": "18:37/q07/p1", "position": "It signals the importance and careful presentation of the ensuing exchange.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī reports al-Irshād's explanation that it alerts the listener to the speech's importance; al-Ālūsī says it presents the exchange as conversation."}, {"id": "18:37/q07/p2", "position": "Its repetition shows the believer's composure, gentle speech, and restraint.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabaʾi says the believer keeps his faith steady, does not insult the man's children, and only hints that his garden may fail."}]}
{"id": "18:37/q08", "question": "What force does the question akafarta have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:37/q08/p1", "position": "It rebukes and censures a disbelief already evident, rather than seeking information.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls it an effective affirmation of disbelief; Ibn ʿAshur adds astonishment and says the speaker knew the man was a polytheist. Thābit's 'woe to you' addition makes the rebuke explicit."}]}
{"id": "18:37/q09", "question": "What is reported in Thābit's expanded wording of the rebuke?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:37/q09/p1", "position": "Thābit adds waylaka, 'woe to you,' before akafarta.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Ālūsī report Thābit al-Bunānī's wording; Abū Ḥayyān calls it explanatory, not a Prophetic reading."}]}
{"id": "18:37/q10", "question": "What disbelief is charged by akafarta?", "turns_on": "Whether the charge targets resurrection doubt, idolatrous association, or the claim that self and natural causes have independent power.", "positions": [{"id": "18:37/q10/p1", "position": "He doubted or denied resurrection, and thereby God's power, truthfulness, or wisdom.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj links doubt after creation to disbelief and false sinful conjecture, citing 38:27; al-Zamakhsharī compares denying a Messenger; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Bursawī stress power; al-Ālūsī prefers this reading and cites 23:115; al-Biqāʿī says the man treated resurrection as a doubtful hypothetical."}, {"id": "18:37/q10/p2", "position": "He associated other beings with God or worshipped idols.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls the rebuke one of association; al-Ālūsī reports an idolatrous reading and notes that calling God 'Lord' does not rule it out; Ibn ʿAshur includes resurrection denial in shirk; al-Qurṭubī infers polytheism from the companion's later refusal to associate anyone."}, {"id": "18:37/q10/p3", "position": "He claimed independence for himself and worldly causes, denying God's sole lordship.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabaʾi says this shirk underlies his doubt about resurrection, though he calls God 'my Lord' and does not outright deny resurrection; human capacities, including mature powers, belong wholly to God."}]}
{"id": "18:37/q11", "question": "What does the question teach about doubt concerning resurrection?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:37/q11/p1", "position": "Doubting resurrection is disbelief in God.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says false conjecture is sinful and cites the warning in 38:27 against treating creation as purposeless; al-Rāzī derives the ruling from the believer's question; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ṭabrisī, and others connect doubt to doubting God's power and attributes."}]}
